summary: Describes additions to ARP that let a station request the protocol address matching a given hardware address, the reverse of normal ARP. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Inverse ARP is a small addition to ARP that lets a machine ask its neighbour for the network address to use for it. It matters on networks such as Frame Relay, where the link tells you the circuit identifier of a connection but not the address of the machine at the other end.

questions: how does inarp work in frame relay
what is inverse arp used for
subtitle: How a station that already knows the link-layer address of its neighbour finds out the network-layer address to use for it.

tldr.problem: On a Frame Relay network a new virtual circuit is announced with its DLCI but no protocol address, so the station that receives the announcement cannot address the other end until someone configures it.
tldr.mechanism: Inverse ARP extends ARP with two operation codes. The station sends a request on the virtual circuit, filling in the hardware address it already knows and zeroing the protocol address it is asking for, and the station at the other end answers with its protocol address.
tldr.outcome: A new circuit becomes usable without configuration and without broadcasting, and the same mechanism works for any network that hands out a destination address without the matching protocol address. The document obsoletes RFC 1293 with only minor changes.

today: RFC 2390 is a Draft Standard from September 1998 that obsoletes RFC 1293, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The changes from the earlier version were minor: the language was formalized, a packet diagram and a worked example were added, and a security section was written.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
As with all Internet mail addresses, the left-hand side, the local part, of an address generated according to this specification is not to be interpreted except by an MTA that handles messages for the domain given in the right-hand side. Since the very first email to GSTN services gateway appeared, implementors have used a number of different methods to specify a GSTN address as an email address. The objectives for these methods have been to enable an email user to access GSTN services from their email interface, and to allow some kind of GSTN over email service transport, possibly reducing the cost of GSTN long distance transmissions, while using the existing email infrastructure.

The document relies heavily on Frame Relay as an example of how Inverse ARP can be useful. It is not, however, intended that InARP be used exclusively with Frame Relay: InARP may be used in any network that provides destination hardware addresses without indicating the corresponding protocol addresses. The opposite problem, allowing a traditional numeric-only GSTN device user to access the email transport service, is not discussed.

The memo replaces RFC 1293. The changes are minor: changes to formalize the language, the addition of a packet diagram and an example in Section 7.2, and a new security section.
sections.plainLanguage: The document relies on Frame Relay as its worked example, but the method is not tied to Frame Relay: it works anywhere the network hands out a destination address without the matching protocol address. The other way round, letting a phone or fax device reach the mail service, is not covered.

sections.title: Why Inverse ARP Exists
sections.content:
The motivation for the development of Inverse ARP comes from the desire to make dynamic address resolution within Frame Relay both possible and efficient. Permanent virtual circuits, and eventually switched virtual circuits, are identified by a Data Link Connection Identifier, and these DLCIs define a single virtual connection through the wide area network and may be thought of as the Frame Relay equivalent of a hardware address. Periodically, through the exchange of signalling messages, a network may announce a new virtual circuit with its corresponding DLCI. Unfortunately, protocol addressing is not included in the announcement. The station receiving such an indication learns of the new connection but cannot address the other side, and without new configuration or a mechanism for discovering the protocol address of the other side, the new virtual circuit is unusable.

Other resolution methods were considered and rejected. Reverse ARP seemed a good candidate, but the response to a request is the protocol address of the requesting station, not of the station receiving the request. IP-specific mechanisms were limiting, since they would not allow the resolution of protocols other than IP. For this reason the ARP protocol was expanded.

Inverse ARP allows a Frame Relay station to discover the protocol address of the station associated with the virtual circuit. It is more efficient than sending ARP messages on every virtual circuit for every address the system wants to resolve, and more flexible than relying on static configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: On Frame Relay the network tells you a connection exists and gives it a number, but not the address of the machine at the other end. Reverse ARP was no use because it answers with the requester's own address, and an IP-only method would not work for other protocols. So ARP itself was extended.

sections.title: The Packet Format
sections.content:
Inverse ARP is an extension of the existing ARP, so it has the same format as standard ARP. The fixed part of the packet carries the hardware type, the protocol type, the byte length of each hardware address, the byte length of each protocol address and the operation code, followed by the source hardware address, the source protocol address, the target hardware address and the target protocol address.

The possible values for the hardware and protocol types are the same as for ARP and are found in the current Assigned Numbers RFC. The length of the hardware and protocol addresses depends on the environment in which InARP is running: if IP is running over Frame Relay, for example, the hardware address length is either 2, 3 or 4 and the protocol address length is 4. The operation code indicates the type of message, request or response: an InARP request is 8 and an InARP response is 9. These values were chosen so as not to conflict with other ARP extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is an ordinary ARP message with two new operation numbers, 8 for a request and 9 for a response, picked so that they would not clash with other uses of ARP.

sections.title: The Exchange
sections.content:
Basic InARP operates essentially the same as ARP, with the exception that InARP does not broadcast requests, because the hardware address of the destination station is already known.

When an interface supporting InARP becomes active, it should initiate the protocol and format InARP requests for each active permanent virtual circuit for which InARP is active. To do this, the requesting station formats a request by inserting its source hardware and source protocol addresses and the known target hardware address, zeroes the target protocol address field, encapsulates the packet for the specific network, and sends it directly to the target station.

On receiving an InARP request, a station may put the requester's protocol address and hardware address mapping into its ARP cache, as it would for any ARP request. Unlike other ARP requests, however, the receiving station may assume that any InARP request it receives is destined for it. For every InARP request the receiving station should format a proper response, using the source addresses from the request as the target addresses of the response. If the station is unable or unwilling to reply, it ignores the request.

When the requesting station receives the InARP response, it may complete the ARP table entry and use the provided address information. As with ARP, information learned via InARP may be aged or invalidated under certain circumstances.
sections.plainLanguage: The request goes straight down the one circuit it is about, with the hardware address it already knows and the protocol address left empty. The station at the other end can assume the request was meant for it, and answers with its own protocol address.

sections.title: Hosts With Several Addresses
sections.content:
A multi-addressed host is a host that has multiple protocol addresses assigned to a single interface. If such a station receives an InARP request, it must choose one address with which to respond. To make the selection, the receiving station must first look at the protocol address of the requesting station, and then respond with the protocol address corresponding to the network of the requester. If the requesting station is probing for an IP address, the responding multi-addressed station should respond with an IP address that corresponds to the same subnet as the requesting station. If the station does not have an address that is appropriate for the request it should not respond: in the IP example, if the receiving station does not have an IP address assigned to the interface that is part of the requested subnet, it would not respond.

A multi-addressed host should send an InARP request for each of the addresses defined for the given interface. The receiving side may, however, answer some or none of those requests depending on its configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: If a machine has several addresses on one interface, it has to pick one to answer with, and the rule is to pick the one that belongs to the same subnet as the machine that asked. If it has no address on that subnet, it stays silent.

sections.title: Inverse ARP over Frame Relay
sections.content:
One case where Inverse ARP can be used is on a Frame Relay interface that supports signalling of DLCIs through a data link management interface. An InARP-equipped station connected to such an interface formats an InARP request and addresses it to the new virtual circuit; if the other side supports InARP, it may return a response indicating the protocol address requested. In a Frame Relay environment, InARP packets are encapsulated using the NLPID and SNAP format that indicates the ARP protocol.

Because DLCIs within most Frame Relay networks have only local significance, an end station does not have a specific DLCI assigned to itself, and so has no address to put into the InARP request or response. The Frame Relay network does provide a method for obtaining the correct DLCIs: the DLCI carried in the Frame Relay header is modified as it traverses the network, so that when the packet arrives at its destination, the DLCI has been set to the value that, from the standpoint of the receiving station, corresponds to the sending station. In the example, if station A sends a message to station B, A places DLCI 50 in the header, and by the time B receives it the network has modified it so that it appears to B as DLCI 70. The correlation between DLCI and Q.922 address is given in a table: DLCI 50 corresponds to 0x0C21, 60 to 0x0CC1, 70 to 0x1061 and 80 to 0x1401. The translation uses a two-octet address in the Q.922 encoding, and for InARP the FECN, BECN, C/R and DE bits are assumed to be zero.

When an InARP message reaches a destination, all the hardware addresses in it are invalid, though the address found in the frame header is correct. Frame Relay may use the address in the header as the sender hardware address, even though this violates the purity of layering. The target hardware address in both the request and the response is also invalid, which causes no problem since InARP does not rely on those fields and an implementation may zero fill or ignore the target hardware address field entirely.

Using the example, station A may use Inverse ARP to discover the protocol address of the station associated with its DLCI 50. The request has the InARP request operation code, an unknown source hardware address, the protocol address of the requesting station, the target hardware address 0x0C21 for DLCI 50 and an unknown target protocol address. When station B receives the packet, it modifies the source hardware address with the Q.922 address from the Frame Relay header, so the request shows 0x1061 for DLCI 70 as the source hardware address. Station B then formats a response and sends it to station A, with the protocol address of B as the source protocol address, the Q.922 address of the requesting station as the target hardware address and the protocol address of the requesting station as the target protocol address. The source hardware address is unknown, and when the response is received station A extracts the address from the Frame Relay header and places it in the source hardware address field, which means the Frame Relay interface must only intervene in the processing of incoming packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Frame Relay rewrites the DLCI in the header as the packet crosses the network, so each side sees its own numbering. The receiving side puts that number into the reply, and the sender reads it back out of the header, so the Frame Relay interface only has to touch the address field on the packets it receives.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document specifies a functional enhancement to the ARP family of protocols, and is subject to the same security constraints that affect ARP and similar address resolution protocols. Because authentication is not a part of ARP, there are known security issues relating to its use, host impersonation among them. No additional security mechanisms have been added to the ARP family of protocols by this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Inverse ARP inherits whatever weaknesses ARP already has, because it adds no authentication of its own. A machine on the network can answer as if it were somebody else.

viz.caption: The problem and the alternatives that were rejected

items.title: The problem
items.text: The network announces a new virtual circuit with its DLCI, but without any protocol address, so the receiving station cannot address the far end.

items.title: Why not Reverse ARP
items.text: Its response carries the protocol address of the requesting station, not of the station that received the request.

items.title: Why not an IP-specific method
items.text: It would not allow the resolution of protocols other than IP.

items.title: Why not configuration
items.text: Sending an ARP message on every circuit for every address would be less efficient, and static configuration is less flexible.
